newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo Brazzaville clashes ease, France reinforces.
newsitem.headline: Congo Brazzaville clashes ease, France reinforces.

text.p: France is more than doubling its forces in Congo-Brazzaville where attempts to promote a truce and dialogue failed to halt a fourth day of fierce fighting between ethnic and political militias.

Sunday's decision to send an extra 500 troops to the volatile capital of the former French colony followed the death of a French soldier in a fire-fight and reports from French nationals who fled the city of hostility towards them there.
Residents and diplomats reported a lull in shooting late on Sunday in the city centre after the capital entered its fourth night under curfew.
"We get the impression it's calming down little by little across the city in general," one diplomat told Reuters.

But despite calls for a truce and dialogue, there was little sign of an end to the ethnic and political rivalry at the heart of the stand-off between President Pascal Lissouba and his allies and former president Denis Sassou Nguesso.

Refugees crossing the river to Kinshasa in Laurent Kabila's Congo on Sunday said the fighting appeared to be more widespread than in 1993, when 2,000 people were killed in the capital following disputed parliamentary elections.
The showdown began on Thursday when troops enforcing a crackdown on private militias in the run-up to a July 27 presidential election surrounded Sassou Nguesso's house.
No reliable death toll was available but police sources said by Saturday that dozens had died.
Lissouba's government accused Sassou Nguesso in a statement on state radio on Sunday of trying to stage a coup and urged the population at large to rally round the security forces.
"The government informs national and international opinion that it's a question of a coup attempt by Denis Sassou Nguesso who once again wants to take power by force of arms," it said.
"The government asks the Congolese people to stay vigilant and support the security forces to save our young democracy."
A spokesman for Sassou Nguesso said that they were simply defending themselves and demanded that Lissouba admit to being the aggressor as a condition for peace talks.

"The aggressor has to recognise that he has committed a serious error before we can go to the negotiating table," Ambrose Noumazalay said by telephone. "It is not a coup d'etat... We haven't attacked, we have only responded."

Sassou Nguesso, a former Marxist military leader, was named president in 1979 but voted out of office in 1992 after the advent of democratic reform. He has accused Lissouba of fomenting violence to postpone the July election.
Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas, runner-up to Lissouba in the 1992 presidential election, heads a national mediation committee. Lissouba has agreed to cooperate with the committee.
Kolelas called on Sunday on state radio for an immediate cease-fire and the arrival of an intervention force to act as a buffer between the rival forces.
His own militia in the Bacongo district was at the heart of fighting in 1993 but has stayed clear this time.

France sent about 450 soldiers to Brazzaville as part of a Western standby operation to evacuate foreign nationals from Kinshasa during the final days of the civil war that brought Kabila to power in what was then Zaire.
The French community in the city numbers about 2,200.
